newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity extends rise on cash, outages.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity extends rise on cash, outages.

text.p: The NYMEX electricity complex settled higher Monday, extending its recent rise on continued strength in cash market prices and generation tightness in the West due to plant outages.
"It's been pretty much cash driven," said a Houston futures trader.
The cash market received an early jolt when power output at the 1,072 megawatt (MW) Diablo Canyon nuclear unit 2 was reduced over the weekend for maintenance work.
The unit, in Avila Beach, Calif., was ramping up to 100 percent power this morning from 29 percent.

Day-ahead firm, peak prices at the California-Oregon Border (COB) jumped $2.00 from Friday to $17.50-19.50 a megawatt hour (MWh), while those at Palo Verde (PV) firmed to $18.50-20.00 from $18.25-19.25 Friday.
May COB settled up 83 cents at $12.89 after posting a session high of $13.00. June COB ended up 38 cents at $12.38. July COB finished up 30 cents at $15.30.
May PV settled up 30 cents at $15.95 after breaching resistance at $15.75 and hitting a high of $16.30. June PV ended up 30 cents at $16.85. Deferred PV contracts finished five to 21 cents higher.
Although the Diablo Canyon outage was brief, the 1,080 MW San Onofre nuclear unit 2 and the 1,158 MW WNP-2 nuclear plant were shut for refueling and maintenance.

Moreover, more than 5,000 MW of coal-fired generation are currently off line for planned and unplanned outages.including the 350 MW San Juan unit in New Mexico and 350 MW Coronado unit in Arizona, where were shut over the weekend.

Nearby contracts' uptrend lent support for rest of the complex, which began to signs of easing last Friday amid growing concerns that there would be above-normal runoffs for hydroelectric generation during the summer.
"There's where most of the action has been. It's stablizing the outer months," said an East Coast electricity broker, referring to the rise of the front-month contracts.
Frigid weather in the Rockies and eastern part of the Northwest in the past several weeks slowed the rate of snowmelt and cut runoffs into the region's hydroelectric dams.
The Northwest was forecast to have mild weather this week, with readings averaging four to eight degrees Fahrenheit above normal regionwide.
In the Southwest, temperatures were called to run eight degrees above normal in the northwest area and five degrees below normal in the southeast section.
